title: Maximum Product of Word Lengths
description: Brute force to optimized: character by character comparison versus 26 bit letter masks.

blocks.text: Given an array of strings, find the maximum possible value of the product of the lengths of two words that do not share any common letters.

blocks.caption: A 26-bit letter mask per word turns a character-by-character comparison into a single AND

blocks.text: Given an array of strings, find the maximum possible value of the product of the lengths of two words that do not share any common letters.

blocks.title: Analogy: Pairing Two Non Overlapping Ingredient Lists
blocks.text: Like pairing up two recipes that use completely different ingredients from each other, and picking the pair whose combined total ingredient count is as large as possible.

blocks.caption: Pick two words sharing no letters at all, maximizing the product of their lengths

blocks.text: Edge case: every word shares at least one letter with every other word
If no valid non overlapping pair exists at all, the answer is 0.

Before comparing characters directly, notice that the actual question, "do these two words share any letter", never cares about a letter's position or how many times it repeats, only whether it appears at all.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Comparing every character of one word against every character of another correctly detects a shared letter, but it repeats the same yes/no membership question over and over, once per character pair, when the true information needed per word is much smaller.

Observation 2: Since the alphabet is fixed at 26 lowercase letters, each word can be summarized completely, for the purpose of "which letters are present", by a single 26-bit number: bit i set means letter i appears somewhere in the word.

Observation 3: Two words share no common letter exactly when their two masks have no bit set in the same position, which is precisely what a bitwise AND detects: if mask1 AND mask2 equals 0, no letter is shared.

Observation 4: Building each word's mask costs only as much as scanning that word once, and after that, checking any pair for a shared letter drops to a single O(1) integer AND, regardless of how long either word actually is.

Whenever a problem only cares about which distinct elements from a small, fixed set are present, not their order or multiplicity, represent each group as a small bitmask and use AND or OR to test overlap in O(1).

This turns the expensive part of the problem, comparing two arbitrarily long words character by character, into a cheap fixed-size integer operation, leaving only the outer loop over pairs as the remaining cost.

Check every pair of words directly, comparing every character of one word against every character of the other to detect any shared letter, and track the largest length product among pairs with no overlap.

items: For every pair of words, compare every character of the first against every character of the second.
If no character matches at all, they share no letters, so consider their length product as a candidate.
Keep the largest such product found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Both inner character loops break immediately the moment any shared letter is found, avoiding any further unnecessary character comparisons once the pair is already known to be invalid.
The length product is only computed and compared for pairs that pass the no-shared-letter check, since an overlapping pair can never contribute to the answer no matter how long it is.
j starts at i + 1, so each unordered pair of words is checked exactly once instead of twice, and a word is never compared against itself.

blocks.text: Every pair of words is directly checked for shared letters, so the true maximum length product among non overlapping pairs is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared times L squared), checking every pair with a nested character comparison, where L is the maximum word length.
Space: O(1) extra, no additional structure is used.

Limitation: comparing every character of one word against every character of another is far more work than necessary, since each word only ever uses letters from a fixed 26 letter alphabet, which can be represented far more compactly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's true cost comes from repeatedly asking the same narrow question, "does this specific character appear in the other word", for every character in one word against every character in the other, for every pair of words. That question only ever has 26 possible distinct answers though, since the alphabet is fixed and small: a word either contains a given letter or it does not. Precomputing, once per word, exactly which of the 26 letters it contains collapses all of that repeated character-level questioning into a single small integer. Comparing two words for shared letters then becomes comparing two integers with a bitwise AND, an operation that takes the same constant time no matter how long the two original words were. The pairwise loop over all words still remains, since there is no way around checking candidate pairs, but the per-pair cost drops from proportional to both words' lengths down to a small constant.

Represent each word as a 26 bit mask, where bit i is set if letter i appears anywhere in that word. Two words share no common letter exactly when their masks AND together to 0, an O(1) check per pair instead of comparing every character combination.
Precompute a 26 bit letter mask for every word, then check pairs using a single AND operation.

blocks.caption: Optimized: a 26 bit mask per word, ANDed together in O(1) to check for shared letters

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), for the pairwise check, plus O(total characters) to build the masks.
Space: O(n), for the array of masks.

A bitmask AND is 0 exactly when no bit position is set in both operands, and since each word's bit position i is set precisely when letter i appears in that word, an AND of 0 between two words' masks is mathematically equivalent to those two words sharing no letter in common, not an approximation or heuristic, an exact restatement of the same fact in bitwise form.

blocks.content: {"headers":["masks[i] & masks[j]","Meaning"],"rows":[["0","The two words share no letter in common; every bit position is set in at most one of the two masks"],["Nonzero","At least one letter appears in both words, since some bit position is set in both masks"]]}

items: mask |= (1 << (ord(ch) - ord('a'))) / mask |= (1 << (ch - 'a')) maps each lowercase letter to its own bit position from 0 (for 'a') to 25 (for 'z'), setting that bit regardless of whether the letter has already been seen in this word.
Every word's mask is computed once, in a separate pass before the pairwise comparison loop begins, so the expensive per-character work happens exactly n times total, not once per pair.
masks[i] & masks[j] == 0 replaces the entire nested character comparison from the brute force with a single machine-word bitwise operation.

blocks.text: Representing a small, fixed alphabet as a bitmask is a recurring technique whenever a problem only cares about which letters are present, not their order or count, since it collapses an expensive character by character comparison down to a single machine word operation.

items: Rebuilding a word's letter mask inside the pairwise comparison loop instead of precomputing every word's mask once up front, which reintroduces repeated work the whole optimization was meant to eliminate.
Confusing "shares no letters" (mask AND equals 0) with some other bitwise condition, like checking for equality or using OR instead of AND, which tests a completely different and incorrect property.
Assuming a nonzero AND result means every letter is shared, when it actually only takes a single overlapping letter to make the AND nonzero, regardless of how many other letters differ.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Words with repeated letters","The bitmask naturally collapses to a single bit regardless of how many times a letter repeats, since OR-ing the same bit twice has no additional effect"],["No valid non-overlapping pair exists at all","The answer correctly stays 0, since best is only ever updated when a qualifying pair is found"]]}

items: Mention that sorting words by length first and breaking early once a remaining candidate could not possibly beat the current best is a minor additional practical pruning on top of the bitmask check, useful for very large inputs.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Two groups or words share no common element" (or the reverse, "share at least one") over a small fixed alphabet or category set signals representing each group as a bitmask and testing overlap with a single AND, instead of comparing elements directly.

items: How would you extend this to find the maximum product among any k mutually non-overlapping words, not just 2? A pairwise AND check no longer suffices directly; this typically needs a search or DP over combinations of masks, since mutual non-overlap among k groups is a stronger condition than any single pairwise check.

What if the alphabet were much larger, say full Unicode, instead of just 26 lowercase letters? A single machine-word bitmask no longer fits; a bitset spanning multiple words, or falling back to a hash set per word, would be needed instead.

Could you avoid the O(n squared) pairwise scan entirely? For this specific maximum-product goal, sorting words by length and applying early-termination pruning helps in practice, but no known technique removes the quadratic worst case entirely for arbitrary letter-overlap patterns.
Same "26-letter alphabet as a bitmask" technique also useful in anagram-adjacent problems and any "which letters appear" style membership check.

Same "turn an expensive per-pair comparison into an O(1) bitwise check" idea as Maximum XOR of Two Numbers' bit trie, both replacing repeated raw comparisons with a precomputed compact representation.
Same general "represent a small fixed-size set as an integer bitmask" idea reused broadly in subset-enumeration and bitmask dynamic programming problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared times L squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (26 bit letter masks): O(n squared) time plus O(total characters) preprocessing, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: 26-bit letter-presence bitmask to test word-pair overlap in O(1)
Core Idea: Represent each word as a bitmask of which letters it contains, then use a bitwise AND to test for any shared letter in constant time
Time: O(n squared) plus O(total characters) to build the masks
Space: O(n), for the array of masks

Most Important Observation: Whenever only the presence of elements from a small, fixed set matters, not their order or count, a bitmask replaces expensive direct comparisons with O(1) bitwise operations
Interview Difficulty: Medium to Hard
One-line memory trick: One word, one bitmask; AND to zero means no shared letters
